title: "Ask them, if they can speak"
hook: the people accuse him, and he tells them to ask the idols, and they fall silent (21:62–65)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the idols and the axe. Ibrahim broke them all and left the biggest standing. Your line was ask the big one. What habit did you question? Day thirty-four.
screen: `THE IDOLS AND THE AXE — ASK THE BIG ONE.`

segments.voice: The festival is over, and the town comes home. Someone walks into the temple and stops dead. Pieces everywhere. Heads on the floor, arms snapped off. And in the middle of the wreckage, the biggest idol, untouched, standing tall. Who did this to our gods? Word goes around. There's a young man who's been talking about them. His name is Ibrahim. Bring him out, they say, in front of everyone, so the whole town can see. You can picture the crowd, the noise, the young man standing in the middle of it. They ask him straight out. And his answer is one of the cleverest lines in the Qur'an.
screen: `THE TOWN COMES HOME.` → `WHO DID THIS TO OUR GODS?` → `BRING HIM OUT, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. They ask: Ibrahim, was it you who did this to our gods? And he points at the big one. In Pickthall's words: “But this, their chief hath done it. So question them, if they can speak.” Ask them. If they can speak. And for a moment, the whole crowd goes quiet. The Qur'an says they turned to one another, and to themselves, and said: surely it's you who are the wrongdoers. That's a real moment of honesty. For one breath, the whole town sees it. Statues that can't say who broke them can't hear a prayer either. And then the next verse says, literally, that they were turned back onto their heads. The old thinking came flooding back. And they said to him: “Well thou knowest that these speak not.” Listen to what they just admitted. They know. They've always known. And Ibrahim asks gently, almost sadly: then do you worship, instead of God, what can neither help you nor harm you? Scholars have long discussed his answer, their chief did it. Was it a lie? A hadith in Bukhari counts it among three times Ibrahim said something not literally true, all of them for God's sake. Many scholars explain it as a pointed kind of irony: said so that the listeners would work out for themselves that it couldn't be true. Because the moment you say, well, it can't speak, you've answered your own question. That's the whole trick. Ibrahim didn't win an argument. He let them hear themselves say it.
screen: `WAS IT YOU, IBRAHIM?` · `QUESTION THEM, IF THEY CAN SPEAK.` · `A MOMENT OF HONESTY, THEN BACK.` · `IRONY, SO THEY'D SEE IT.` · then, large: `THEY CANNOT SPEAK.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Think of something you give power to that has none. A number on a scale. A like count. An old voice from school that still tells you what you are. A superstition you half believe. Picture it in the middle of the room, like the big idol. Now ask it Ibrahim's question: can you speak? Can you help me? Can you harm me, really? Listen to the silence. If you pray, you can turn toward the One who hears. The bell holds the time.
Ask them. Ibrahim's answer to the crowd: question the idols, if they can speak. And the town admits they cannot.
Your line: they cannot speak. Today, notice one thing you give power to that has none, and say it out loud to yourself: it can't speak. Day thirty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims read Ibrahim's questioning of the idols as a model of patient reasoning, and teachers use his words to invite people to think honestly about what they rely on.

original.note: Arabic: "so ask them, if they can speak" (21:63).

trapdoor: what you thought: Abraham told a lie to get out of trouble.
what it means: ask them — Ibrahim points to the idol so the crowd has to say it themselves: they cannot speak.

what a scholar hears: a hadith in Bukhari counts it among three sayings of Ibrahim not literally true, all for God's sake; scholars call it ta'rid, pointed irony; and 21:65 says they were turned back onto their heads.

sources.ref: Qur'an 21:59–62, 64, 66–67 (the accusation; the moment of honesty; neither help nor harm)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3358 (Ibrahim's three statements for God's sake)

notes: Pickthall 21:63 and 21:65 quoted from memory; confirm (21:65: 'And they were utterly confounded, and they said: Well thou knowest that these speak not.').
21:64 ('Then gathered they apart and said: Lo! ye yourselves are the wrong-doers') paraphrased; commentators read 'returned to themselves' as an inner moment of recognition. Confirm.
21:65 nukisu 'ala ru'usihim ('turned back onto their heads') paraphrased; Pickthall renders it 'utterly confounded'.
Bukhari 3358 and the ta'rid explanation: a sensitive point (whether a prophet can lie). The script gives the hadith and the mainstream explanation. A Keeper should check the wording.
